Part II — Workflow Flows

This part walks through the most common real-world sign-off workflows a CFI performs — from a student pilot's pre-solo prerequisites and first solo to checkride packages, flight reviews, and aircraft endorsements. Each numbered step names the exact AC 61-65K endorsement used at that point and links straight to its full card in Part I, so you can jump from the workflow to the verbatim endorsement language and back. Supplemental endorsements that are commonly signed in the same sitting are listed under "Also commonly included."

Pre-Solo

Student Pilot

Student pilot prerequisites before first solo: TSA eligibility, student pilot certificate, and medical qualification.

Before most airplane students can exercise PIC solo privileges, they need a student pilot certificate, required medical qualification, and the pre-solo training endorsements. Dual instruction may begin before these are fully in place.

Before the first solo — T · I · M

T TSA citizenship / eligibility verification

Flight training providers must handle TSA citizenship or eligibility verification when applicable. If the logbook-endorsement method is used, AC 61-65K A.14 provides commonly used language.

49 CFR § 1552.15(c) AC 61-65K, A.14
I Student pilot certificate application

Apply through IACRA or an acceptable paper process with an authorized person such as a CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO representative. It is not an IACRA-only process.

14 CFR § 61.83 14 CFR § 61.85
M Medical certificate / qualifying medical status

For most private-path airplane students, solo requires at least a third-class medical or another qualifying medical basis that fits the operation being conducted.

14 CFR § 61.3(c) 14 CFR § 61.23

TSA Citizenship / Eligibility

TSA citizenship or eligibility verification is a training-provider compliance item and is separate from the FAA student pilot certificate and separate from medical qualification.

Key Points

  • Training providers must follow applicable TSA citizenship or eligibility verification procedures before providing covered flight training
  • If the provider uses the logbook-endorsement method for U.S. citizenship verification, AC 61-65K A.14 contains commonly used endorsement language
  • This step does not replace the student pilot certificate and does not replace the required medical qualification

Student Pilot Certificate

A student pilot certificate is required before solo flight, but it is not required to begin dual flight instruction.

Eligibility

  • Minimum age 16 for airplane (14 for glider or balloon)
  • Must be able to read, speak, write, and understand English

Application Process

  • Application may be made through IACRA (iacra.faa.gov) or by paper in a form acceptable to the Administrator — 14 CFR 61.85 does not limit the method to IACRA only
  • An authorized person (CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO representative) verifies identity and processes or forwards the application as required
  • The FAA does not charge a fee when the certificate is processed through a FSDO; a school, examiner, or other processing entity may charge its own fee

Certificate Issuance & Duration

  • The permanent certificate is mailed; a temporary student pilot certificate may become available in the applicant's IACRA console after processing
  • Student pilot certificates issued after April 1, 2016 no longer expire in the old 24/36-month way — they are generally surrendered when upgrading to a higher certificate
  • Solo endorsements are placed in the logbook, not printed on the student pilot certificate itself

Documents to Carry on Solo Flight

  • Student pilot certificate
  • Photo identification
  • Medical certificate or other qualifying documentation as applicable

Medical Certificate

A separate medical qualification is generally required before solo flight for the normal airplane/private training path. The student pilot certificate and medical qualification are separate requirements and should not be confused.

  • Third-class medical is the typical requirement for most student pilots training toward private or recreational airplane privileges
  • Medical class depends on the privileges being exercised — not simply the highest certificate a pilot may someday hold
  • Commercial privileges generally require at least a second-class medical when those privileges are exercised
  • ATP PIC privileges generally require a first-class medical when those privileges are exercised
  • Some students may qualify under exceptions or different pathways (sport pilot, glider/balloon, certain 61.113(i) operations)

How to Obtain a Medical

  1. Complete the MedXPress application online before your appointment
  2. Schedule an exam with an FAA-designated Aviation Medical Examiner (AME)
  3. Obtain the medical early — do not let it delay solo training

Solo Timeline

  1. Start dual instruction
  2. Apply for the student pilot certificate
  3. Complete TSA citizenship/eligibility verification if applicable
  4. Obtain the required medical qualification
  5. Complete pre-solo aeronautical knowledge test and flight training
  6. Receive the appropriate solo endorsements
  7. Exercise solo privileges only when all required elements are satisfied

Solo privileges may be exercised only when these prerequisites and applicable endorsements are satisfied.

First Solo

Student Pilot

Initial daytime solo package for a student pilot.

  1. A.3 Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge

    Used before first solo to confirm the student passed the required pre-solo knowledge test for that make and model.

  2. A.4 Pre-solo flight training

    Shows the student received the required pre-solo flight training and is proficient in that make and model.

  3. A.6 Solo flight (first 90-calendar-day period)

    Authorizes the student’s first solo flights in a specific make and model. Must be given by the instructor who trained the student and expires in 90 calendar days.

Also commonly included A.14 — Endorsement of U.S. citizenship recommended by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA)

Also include if you are using the TSA citizenship logbook endorsement method.

Open this category in Part I →

Initial Solo XC

Student Pilot

Initial solo cross-country package with per-flight planning review.

  1. A.9 Solo cross-country flight

    Gives the student the initial solo cross-country endorsement package for that category, make, and model.

  2. A.10 Solo cross-country flight

    Shows the instructor reviewed and approved planning for a specific solo cross-country flight. Required before each solo XC flight.

Instrument Checkride Bundle

Instrument Rating

Common Part 61 instrument practical test package.

  1. A.43 Flight proficiency/practical test

    Shows the applicant completed the required training and is proficient for the flight proficiency or practical test.

  2. A.44 Prerequisites for instrument practical tests

    Combines the instrument practical-test recommendation with review of knowledge-test deficiencies. Valid for 2 calendar months.

Also commonly included A.1 — Prerequisites for practical test

Also commonly included for a typical instrument practical test package.

CFI ASEL Initial Checkride Bundle

Flight Instructor

Common Part 61 Airplane Single-Engine Land initial flight instructor practical test package.

  1. A.47 Flight instructor ground and flight proficiency/practical test

    Shows the applicant completed the required training and is proficient for the flight instructor practical test.

  2. A.49 Spin training

    Documents the required spin training for the applicable flight instructor applicant.

Also commonly included A.46 — Flight instructor aeronautical knowledge test A.45 — Fundamentals of instructing knowledge test A.2 — Review of deficiencies identified on airman knowledge test A.1 — Prerequisites for practical test

Also commonly included for a typical CFI ASEL initial practical test package.

Flight Review and WINGS

Additional / Recurrent

Flight review completion and WINGS phase completion endorsements.

  1. A.69 Completion of a flight review

    Shows a flight review is complete and the instructor found the pilot able to safely use certificate privileges.

  2. A.70 Completion of any phase of an FAA-sponsored Pilot Proficiency Program (WINGS)

    Documents completion of a qualifying WINGS phase that can substitute for a flight review.
